title: Pre-start hazard assessment
audience: Trainee or new worker on the pressure cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Assess injection injuries, slips, pedestrians, flying debris, wind, traffic, overhead electricity and operating environment.

instruction.heading: Injection injury is the first hazard to assess
instruction.body: The pre-start assessment is the point where the hazards of the job are named before any equipment is switched on. For pressure work, the first hazard is the water itself. WorkSafe Victoria's alert on high-pressure water jetting says a water jet can pierce the skin, and that contaminated material may be injected into the body. The same alert sets the expectation for controls. Anyone near jetting operations should wear eye protection, and the operator who controls the water flow should wear, at minimum, safety glasses and a face shield. Head protection is to be worn where needed, leg and body armour that can withstand the jet's direct force is needed where there is a risk of injury from the jet, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled. Whatever the work, a jet that pierces skin is a medical emergency. Get urgent medical attention, and record the time and the event.

instruction.heading: Slips, pedestrians, traffic and debris
instruction.body: Wet hard surfaces, drips from the equipment, and water that runs off into a footpath or driveway are slip hazards. Walk the area on a fixed route before setup and note the surfaces that will be wet, the edges that drop away, the steps, and the places where a worker could be pushed off balance by the recoil of the lance. Pedestrians, including children and people with a mobility or sight impairment, may not see a spray zone. Set up an exclusion zone wide enough that the spray and the runoff stay inside it, and keep the zone closed while work continues. If the work is beside a road, the traffic risk is separate from the pedestrian risk. Flying debris from loose paint, grit, leaves and fragments of old sealant can strike people and vehicles. Check for loose material before the first pass and keep people back from the area the debris can reach.

instruction.heading: Wind, weather and overhead electricity
instruction.body: Wind changes the spray path and can carry overspray over people, vehicles and windows. Stop and reassess when a gust changes the direction or force of the spray, and do not work into a wind that carries spray toward others. Rain makes surfaces more slippery and can change the risk to electrical equipment. Water conducts electricity, so the risk of electric shock rises when equipment is used near water. A Queensland safety alert says equipment used near water should be connected to a safety switch or a residual current device, or fitted with a portable RCD. The same alert says a portable RCD should be tested before each use, or daily, whichever is the longer interval, and inspected every three months by a competent person. Check the position of overhead lines before any hose or lance is raised. In New South Wales, the SafeWork NSW code on work near overhead and underground electric lines (in force from 22 May 2026) sets 3.0 m for ordinary persons near lines up to 132,000 V, and 4.0 m for conductive materials near low-voltage overhead service lines. A wet hose, lance or water jet can conduct, so this course applies the 4.0 m figure near low-voltage lines; that is a course decision, not a figure the code gives for water. Refer to the network operator, and do not work closer to an overhead line than the network operator allows.

instruction.heading: The operating environment and the risk assessment
instruction.body: Look at the whole environment, not only the surface to be cleaned. Note the drains and where the runoff will go, the location of emergency exits and first-aid access, the lighting, the traction on the ground, the hose route and any place where a hose can be trapped or damaged. Ask about pets, unsecured doors and gates, and any chemicals stored nearby. For each hazard, assess how likely it is and how serious the outcome could be, then decide the control, name the person responsible for it, and set the trigger that stops the work. A risk assessment that names no owner and no stop trigger is not a finished assessment. Recheck the assessment whenever the site changes, when the weather changes, or when a new person arrives. Noise also needs assessment. The exposure standard is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled.

instruction.heading: Elevated work and the competency boundary
instruction.body: If the job requires work above ground level, the fall risk is a separate hazard to assess before the work begins. Safe Work Australia treats construction work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres as high risk, and the control order starts with keeping work on the ground or a solid construction. In New South Wales a safe work method statement is needed where a fall could be more than 2 metres. Any elevated work must be authorised in writing and carried out by a person with the licence the state requires. This lesson does not grant that authority, and it does not grant authority for regulated high-pressure jetting, electrical isolation or confined-space work. Where a task exceeds the trainee's authority, stop and escalate it to the supervisor.

procedure: Walk the site on a fixed route, and note the surfaces, the steps, the drains, the access points and the people or animals present.
Identify the injection hazard and the PPE the operator and bystanders must wear, following the WorkSafe Victoria alert, before the equipment is unloaded.
Set the exclusion zone for spray, runoff and debris, and plan how pedestrians and children will be kept out of it.
Check the wind, the weather and the traction on the ground, and decide whether the work can start or must wait.
Check the position of overhead lines and any electrical equipment, and confirm that equipment near water has the required safety switch or portable RCD.
Identify traffic and road exposure, and confirm the traffic control plan for the road, or stop if it is not in place.
Write the risk assessment: for each hazard, name the control, the responsible person and the stop trigger.
Brief the team and the on-site contact, and recheck the assessment whenever the site, the weather or the people change.

workedExamples.situation: A school courtyard is quiet during setup, but the class dismissal starts halfway through the job. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which control protects the children, and when do you stop?
workedExamples.reasoning: The pre-start assessment should have included the dismissal time, because the exclusion zone cannot be kept secure once children are leaving. Revise the timing so that the spray work finishes before dismissal, or suspend the work until the courtyard is clear and the zone can be held. Record the timing decision, the person who made it, and the stop trigger, which is any child or adult entering the zone.

workedExamples.situation: A gust rises across a hard surface while a team works near a parked car and a footpath. This is an example job.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the spray, make the area safe, and move the spray away from people and vehicles. Reassess the wind and the exclusion zone before resuming. Do not keep working because the gust is brief, and do not raise the pressure to finish sooner. Record the change in conditions and the decision to resume or postpone.

workedExamples.situation: A hose route would pass under overhead service lines to reach the back of a yard. This is an example job.
workedExamples.reasoning: Not as planned. In New South Wales, the code does not state a figure for water-fed hoses; the 4.0 m figure for conductive materials near low-voltage lines is applied here as a precaution, so the route must keep the hose and the operator at least that far from the lines. Choose a route that keeps the hose and the operator clear of the lines, or refer the job. Record the route decision and the referral. Do not use the route without the network operator's advice.

equipmentAndPpe: Safety glasses and a face shield for the operator controlling water flow, as the WorkSafe Victoria alert describes
Eye protection for anyone near the jetting or cleaning activity
Head protection where a falling or striking hazard exists, and leg and body protection where the jet presents a direct risk
Hearing protection where noise cannot be controlled
Non-slip footwear and high-visibility clothing for the team and the spotter
Barrier tape, cones and signage for the exclusion zone
A portable RCD or a safety switch for equipment used near water, tested at the interval the guidance sets
First-aid kit and a list of emergency contacts on site

commonErrors.error: Assessing only the surface being cleaned and not the surroundings.
commonErrors.prevention: Walk the whole environment, including the footpath, the drains, the traffic and the people.

commonErrors.error: Starting the work during a quiet period without checking the timing of the day.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the timing of school, shop and traffic activity, and revise the plan before setup.

commonErrors.error: Treating PPE as the main control.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the exclusion zone, the wind check and the stop triggers first, and use PPE as the last layer.

commonErrors.error: Continuing work after a gust, a pedestrian or a change in the surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the stop triggers into the assessment, and stop when one is met.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Injection hazard and PPE: the WorkSafe Victoria alert sets out the PPE expectations described in the instruction, says modification of equipment needs written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person, and says operators must be trained and assessed through a registered training organisation for Class B equipment.

Electrical equipment near water: a safety switch or portable RCD is recommended, with testing at the interval the Queensland alert gives. That alert concerns inflatable balls, so its points are applied here by analogy.

Height: work with a fall risk of more than 2 metres is high risk construction work, and New South Wales requires a safe work method statement above that height. Elevated work needs written authorisation and any licence the state requires. This lesson does not grant either.
Noise: the exposure standard is 85 decibels as an average over eight hours, and hearing protection is needed where noise cannot be controlled.

qualityStandard: The risk assessment names each hazard in the outcome: injection, slips, pedestrians, debris, wind, traffic, overhead electricity and the operating environment.
Each hazard has a control, a responsible person and a stop trigger, and the assessment is signed before setup.
The exclusion zone is marked, and pedestrians and children are kept out of it.
The assessment is rechecked when conditions change, and the change is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Pre-start risk assessment naming each significant hazard, control, residual concern and owner
Site plan showing the exclusion zone, the access route, the drains and any overhead line
Record of PPE issued and the briefing given to the team and the on-site contact
Log of each stop, the reason, and the decision to resume or postpone
summary: Name the injection hazard first, and set the PPE the WorkSafe Victoria alert describes.
Assess slips, pedestrians, traffic, debris, wind and overhead electricity before setup, and set a stop trigger for each.

Use an RCD for electrical equipment near water. Apply the NSW overhead line clearances (3.0 m and 4.0 m) in New South Wales. In Victoria, the official no-go zone is 3 m, with a registered spotter from 3 m to 6.4 m. In Queensland, the WorkSafe exclusion zone for lines up to 132 kV is 3 m. Refer any other state's clearance to the network operator.
Recheck the assessment whenever the site, the weather or the people change.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the WorkSafe Victoria alert say about the operator who controls the water flow?
options: At minimum, safety glasses and a face shield
No eye protection is needed if the operator stands back
Ear protection is the only requirement

knowledgeChecks.question: Equipment is to be used near water. What is recommended?
options: Use any extension lead if it is dry on the outside and looks fine, since the water will not reach the plug at all
Connect the equipment to a safety switch or portable RCD, and test it at the interval the guidance sets
Ignore the RCD for a short job, since the work will be finished quickly and the cord stays dry
Keep the cord in the water to reduce trips over the hose on the ground and the path nearby

knowledgeChecks.question: A gust rises while the team is working near a footpath. What is the best response?
options: Keep working, because the gust is brief and the spray will settle quickly once it passes
Stop, make the area safe, move the spray away from people and vehicles, and reassess before resuming
Increase the pressure to finish quickly before the wind gets any stronger on the day today
Ask pedestrians to walk through the spray, since they are passing anyway and it is brief
